The problem concerns a result from the theory of finite simple groups related to the generalized Baer–Suzuki theorem: given a sporadic simple group $S$, an automorphism $x\in\operatorname{Aut}(S)$ of order $>2$, and a prime $r\mid |S|$ with $(r,|x|)=1$, one asks for the smallest number $N(S,x,r)$ of conjugates of $x$ needed to generate a subgroup whose order is divisible by $r$.

For finite simple groups, a deep theorem (established using the Classification and detailed analysis of maximal subgroups and character theory of sporadic groups) asserts that three conjugates always suffice, i.e. $N(S,x,r)\le 3$, with precisely one exceptional triple $(S,x^{\operatorname{Aut}(S)},r)$ where the bound fails and one needs exactly four conjugates.

The obstruction in the exceptional case arises from the $2$-local structure of the group: $x$ has odd order and the hardest prime to "reach" by products of conjugates of an odd-order element is $r=2$. In the unique sporadic exceptional configuration (involving the Baby Monster $\mathbb{B}$ and a specific conjugacy class of elements of order $3$), every triple of conjugates of $x$ generates a subgroup of odd order, so a fourth conjugate is required to obtain a subgroup of even order. No other sporadic triple exhibits this behavior, and for all other primes $r$ the bound $3$ holds.

Thus the prime in the exceptional case is

\boxed{2}
